Competitive breaking, in which dancers, known as b-boys and b-girls, face off in structured battles judged on creativity, technique, musicality and originality, developed its own competitive circuit over subsequent decades, with dancers combining acrobatic power moves, intricate footwork and freezes, in which a dancer holds a striking pose, often upside down or in an unusual balance.

Breaking made its Olympic debut at the Paris 2024 Games, marking the first time a dance-based discipline had been included as a medal sport at the Olympics, reflecting the same push toward including youth-oriented, culturally rooted sports that also brought skateboarding and sport climbing into the Olympic programme.

articles.title: Horse Racing
articles.description: One of the oldest spectator sports in the world.
articles.content:
Horse racing, in which horses ridden by jockeys compete over a set distance, is one of the oldest organised spectator sports in the world, with archaeological and historical evidence of organised racing found in ancient civilisations including Greece, Rome and across Central Asia, where horsemanship held deep cultural significance.

Modern thoroughbred flat racing traces much of its organisational structure to England, where formal rules and the tracking of horse pedigrees developed from the 17th and 18th centuries onward, eventually producing famous annual events such as the Kentucky Derby in the United States, first run in 1875, and Royal Ascot in England, attended by British royalty since the early 18th century.

Beyond flat racing, other forms include steeplechase racing, in which horses jump obstacles over the course, and harness racing, in which a horse pulls a driver in a light cart at a controlled trot or pace, each with its own dedicated following in different countries around the world.

articles.title: Polo
articles.description: The ancient mounted ball game of Central Asia.
articles.content:
Polo is a team sport played on horseback, in which mounted players use long-handled mallets to strike a ball and attempt to score goals, one of the oldest team sports still played today. Its roots trace back over two thousand years to Central Asia and Persia, where it is believed to have originated as a form of cavalry training before becoming a sport enjoyed by nobility across the region.

The sport spread widely across Asia over the centuries, including into the Indian subcontinent, where it was later encountered and adopted by British colonists in the 19th century, who helped codify modern rules and spread the sport to Europe, the Americas and beyond.

A related and much older Central Asian and Caucasian game, chovgan, still played traditionally in Azerbaijan, shares many similarities with polo and reflects the deep, ancient regional roots that mounted ball games have across this part of the world, a heritage recognised internationally through cultural preservation efforts.

articles.title: Chovgan
articles.description: Azerbaijan's traditional horseback ball game.
articles.content:
Chovgan is a traditional equestrian team sport from Azerbaijan, in which mounted players use long mallets to strike a ball and score goals against an opposing team, closely related to the broader family of mounted ball games, including polo, that developed across Central Asia, Persia and the Caucasus over many centuries.

The game has deep historical roots in Azerbaijani and wider Caucasian culture, historically associated with training in horsemanship, coordination and courage, and it was traditionally played in the Karabakh region, an area also renowned for producing the Karabakh horse, a breed particularly prized for its agility and endurance, qualities well suited to the fast, close-contact nature of the game.

UNESCO inscribed chovgan, traditional Karabakh horse-riding game in the Republic of Azerbaijan, on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2013, recognising its cultural significance, and Azerbaijan has worked in subsequent years to help preserve and revive the tradition through dedicated tournaments and cultural events.

articles.title: Mixed Martial Arts
articles.description: The full-contact combat sport combining multiple disciplines.
articles.content:
Mixed martial arts, commonly abbreviated as MMA, is a full-contact combat sport that allows competitors to use techniques drawn from a wide range of fighting disciplines, including boxing, wrestling, judo, Brazilian jiu-jitsu and Muay Thai, fought both standing and on the ground within a single unified rule set.

The sport's modern form is often traced to the first Ultimate Fighting Championship event, held in the United States in 1993, which was initially promoted as a contest to determine which traditional martial art was most effective in a real fight, pitting practitioners of different disciplines directly against one another with comparatively few rules.

Over subsequent decades the sport developed far more comprehensive safety rules, weight classes and regulatory oversight similar to other combat sports such as boxing, and it has grown into one of the fastest-growing sports worldwide, with organisations such as the UFC drawing large global television and streaming audiences for its events.

articles.title: Rally Racing
articles.description: Motorsport competition on closed public roads.
articles.content:
Rally racing, or rallying, is a form of motorsport in which competitors drive modified road-legal or specially built cars over a course made up of closed public or forest roads, typically racing against the clock individually rather than directly against other competitors on the track at the same time, unlike most other forms of racing.

A driver is usually accompanied by a co-driver, who reads detailed pre-recorded notes describing the upcoming twists, jumps and hazards of the route, allowing the driver to anticipate the road ahead at high speed even on unfamiliar terrain, since rally stages often cross varied and challenging surfaces including gravel, tarmac, snow and ice depending on the location and season.

The World Rally Championship, established in 1973, is the sport's premier international series, featuring events held in a wide variety of countries and terrains, and rallying has historically produced some of motorsport's most demanding tests of both driver skill and vehicle durability under punishing conditions.

articles.title: Paragliding
articles.description: Free flight with a fabric wing.
articles.content:
Paragliding is an adventure sport and form of free flight in which a pilot is suspended in a harness beneath a large fabric wing, similar in principle to a parachute but specifically designed to generate lift and allow sustained, controlled flight rather than simply descending. The sport developed from parachuting in the 1970s and 1980s as pilots and designers refined wing shapes specifically to allow gliding and soaring flight from mountainsides and hills.

Pilots launch typically by running down a slope until the wing inflates and generates enough lift to carry them into the air, and skilled paraglider pilots can use rising air currents, known as thermals, to gain altitude and remain airborne for extended periods, sometimes travelling considerable cross-country distances entirely under the power of the wind and rising air alone.

Paragliding equipment is comparatively lightweight, compact and portable compared with other forms of powered or unpowered flight, which has helped make the sport increasingly accessible to enthusiasts around the world, including in mountainous regions well suited to launching, such as parts of the Caucasus.

articles.title: Motocross
articles.description: Off-road motorcycle racing over rough terrain.
articles.content:
Motocross is a form of off-road motorcycle racing conducted on natural or purpose-built dirt tracks featuring jumps, sharp turns and rough, often changing terrain designed to test both the rider's skill and the durability of the specially built motorcycles used in competition. The sport traces its origins to motorcycle trials and scrambling races held in Britain in the early 20th century.

Races typically involve multiple riders competing simultaneously on the same track, requiring not only speed but also the ability to navigate closely alongside competitors over demanding jumps and rough surfaces, making close contact and occasional collisions a recognised part of the sport's inherent risk and appeal.

Motocross has grown into a significant global sport with major professional championships, including the FIM Motocross World Championship, and has also inspired related disciplines such as supercross, held in large indoor stadiums on artificially constructed dirt courses, and freestyle motocross, which emphasises aerial tricks over pure racing speed.

articles.title: Lionel Messi
articles.description: The Argentine forward regarded as one of football's all-time greats.
articles.content:
Lionel Messi, born in Rosario, Argentina, in 1987, is widely considered one of the greatest footballers in the history of the sport, celebrated for his close ball control, vision and remarkable consistency in scoring and creating goals over an unusually long career at the highest level.

He spent the majority of his career at Barcelona, where he rose through the club's famous youth academy after moving to Spain as a child to receive treatment for a growth hormone condition, and went on to win numerous domestic and European titles while repeatedly breaking individual scoring records and winning the Ballon d'Or, awarded annually to the world's best player, more times than any other player in history.

After moving to Paris Saint-Germain and later Inter Miami in the United States, Messi achieved the one major honour that had eluded him for years, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, a triumph widely regarded as the crowning achievement of an extraordinary career.

articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo
articles.description: The Portuguese forward known for his goal-scoring records.
articles.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo, born on the Portuguese island of Madeira in 1985, is one of the most successful and recognisable footballers in the history of the sport, known for his combination of athleticism, powerful finishing and remarkable longevity at the top level of the game well into his late thirties.

He rose to international prominence at Manchester United before moving to Real Madrid, where he became the club's all-time leading goalscorer and won multiple European Champions League titles, later playing for Juventus in Italy before returning to Manchester United and eventually moving to Saudi Arabia's Al Nassr, extending his career and drawing significant international attention to football in the region.

Ronaldo has won the Ballon d'Or on multiple occasions and holds numerous individual scoring records at both club and international level, including becoming the leading goalscorer in men's international football history with Portugal, and his long-running rivalry with Lionel Messi is often considered one of the defining storylines of modern football.

articles.title: Serena Williams
articles.description: The American player who dominated women's tennis for two decades.
articles.content:
Serena Williams, born in the United States in 1981, is widely regarded as one of the greatest tennis players in history, having won 23 Grand Slam singles titles during a professional career that spanned more than two decades, a period in which she and her sister Venus Williams transformed the sport's visibility and popularity.

Trained from a young age by her father, Richard Williams, alongside her sister Venus in Compton, California, Serena turned professional in 1995 and went on to dominate women's tennis with a powerful serve and aggressive playing style, winning major titles across all four Grand Slam tournaments multiple times and holding the world number one ranking for extended periods throughout her career.

Beyond her playing achievements, Williams became an influential cultural figure, using her platform to speak on issues including gender and racial equality in sport, and she continued competing at an elite level well into motherhood, announcing her retirement from professional tennis in 2022 after a career that redefined expectations for longevity and dominance in the sport.

articles.title: Michael Jordan
articles.description: The basketball player who redefined the sport's global appeal.
articles.content:
Michael Jordan, born in the United States in 1963, is widely regarded as one of the greatest basketball players in history and a figure whose influence extended far beyond the sport itself, helping to transform basketball into a genuinely global phenomenon during his playing career with the Chicago Bulls.

Jordan led the Bulls to six NBA championships during the 1990s, earning numerous individual awards along the way, and became renowned for his competitive intensity, scoring ability and clutch performances in high-pressure moments, cementing his reputation as one of the sport's defining figures of the era.

His partnership with the sportswear company Nike, which launched the enormously successful Air Jordan sneaker line in 1984, is often credited with transforming the relationship between professional athletes and consumer brands, establishing a model of athlete endorsement and commercial influence that shaped how sports marketing developed in the decades that followed.

articles.title: Muhammad Ali
articles.description: The boxer known as much for his words as his fists.
articles.content:
Muhammad Ali, born Cassius Clay in the United States in 1942, was a heavyweight boxer widely regarded as one of the greatest athletes of the 20th century, known both for his exceptional speed and skill in the ring and for his outspoken personality and social and political activism outside it.

He won Olympic gold as a light heavyweight in 1960 before turning professional, later winning the world heavyweight title three separate times, a feat previously unmatched. His refusal to be drafted into the United States military during the Vietnam War, on religious and moral grounds after converting to Islam and changing his name, led to him being stripped of his boxing titles for several years, a decision widely seen in retrospect as unjust.

Ali's fights, including legendary bouts known as the Rumble in the Jungle and the Thrilla in Manila, became cultural touchstones, and his combination of athletic brilliance, verbal wit and willingness to take unpopular political stands made him one of the most influential sporting figures of his era, extending his legacy well beyond boxing itself.

articles.title: LeBron James
articles.description: The basketball star known for extraordinary career longevity.
articles.content:
LeBron James, born in the United States in 1984, is widely regarded as one of the greatest basketball players in history, notable both for his combination of size, skill and basketball intelligence and for an unusually long career sustained at an elite level well into his late thirties and beyond.

James entered the NBA directly from high school in 2003 amid enormous media anticipation and went on to win multiple championships across stints with several different teams, including the Cleveland Cavaliers, Miami Heat and Los Angeles Lakers, becoming the league's all-time leading scorer, surpassing a record that had stood for decades.

Beyond basketball, James has been an influential and outspoken figure on social and political issues, invested in education initiatives in his hometown of Akron, Ohio, and built a significant media and business portfolio, reflecting a broader trend of modern elite athletes expanding their influence well beyond their sport.

articles.title: Simone Biles
articles.description: The gymnast who redefined the limits of the sport.
articles.content:
Simone Biles, born in the United States in 1997, is widely regarded as the greatest gymnast in history, having won an unprecedented number of world and Olympic medals while performing skills of such difficulty that several have been named after her in the sport's official scoring code, since she was the first gymnast ever to successfully complete them in competition.

Raised by her grandparents after a childhood marked by early instability, Biles rose through the American gymnastics system to dominate international competition from the mid-2010s onward, combining exceptional power, precision and consistency across all four women's Olympic apparatus.

At the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, Biles withdrew from several events citing mental health concerns and a phenomenon known in gymnastics as the twisties, in which a gymnast temporarily loses spatial awareness mid-air, a decision that was widely praised for drawing attention to athlete mental health, and she returned to further Olympic success at the Paris 2024 Games.

articles.title: Roger Federer
articles.description: The Swiss player celebrated for his graceful playing style.
articles.content:
Roger Federer, born in Switzerland in 1981, is widely regarded as one of the greatest tennis players in history, celebrated in particular for the elegance and apparent effortlessness of his playing style, which combined precise technique with remarkable court coverage and shot-making.

Federer won 20 Grand Slam singles titles over the course of his career and held the world number one ranking for a record total number of weeks, establishing a long rivalry with fellow greats Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic that came to define men's tennis for much of the 2000s and 2010s, with matches between the three widely regarded among the finest in the sport's history.

Known for his sportsmanship and popularity with fans around the world, Federer announced his retirement from professional tennis in 2022, and he has remained involved in the sport through business ventures, philanthropy focused on education in Africa, and his continued presence at major tennis events as a widely respected elder statesman of the game.

articles.title: Sports Equipment and Technology
articles.description: How innovation has changed how athletes compete.
articles.content:
Advances in materials science and engineering have transformed sporting equipment over the past century, often significantly changing how sports are played and what levels of performance are achievable. Lightweight carbon fibre has replaced wood and metal in equipment ranging from tennis racket frames and bicycle wheels to Formula 1 car bodies, allowing for stronger yet lighter designs than earlier materials permitted.

In some cases, equipment innovation has proven so effective that governing bodies have chosen to restrict or ban certain technologies to preserve fair and consistent competition: full-body polyurethane swimsuits, which reduced drag and contributed to a wave of broken world records at the 2008 Beijing Olympics, were subsequently banned from competitive swimming from 2010 onward.

Wearable technology, including heart rate monitors, GPS trackers and, increasingly, sensors embedded directly in equipment, now allows athletes and coaches to gather detailed real-time data on performance and physical exertion during both training and competition, reflecting a broader shift toward data-driven approaches across many different sports.

articles.title: World Records in Sport
articles.description: The pursuit of the fastest, highest and strongest.
articles.content:
A world record in sport is an officially recognised best performance ever achieved in a given event, typically verified and maintained by the relevant international governing body for that sport. Some of the most closely followed world records include those in athletics events such as the 100 metres sprint and the marathon, where even small improvements attract significant public and media attention.

Records are broken through a combination of factors, including advances in training science, nutrition and equipment technology, improved competition conditions such as purpose-built tracks and pacing strategies, and, occasionally, genuinely exceptional individual athletic talent, making it often difficult to separate how much of a record-breaking performance reflects the athlete versus the surrounding conditions.

Some world records have proven remarkably durable, standing for many years or even decades, while others in certain events are broken repeatedly within relatively short periods, and governing bodies maintain strict verification procedures, including drug testing, to ensure that record-breaking performances are considered legitimate.

articles.title: Youth Sports
articles.description: How children and teenagers get involved in organised sport.
articles.content:
Youth sports refer to organised athletic activities for children and teenagers, ranging from informal community and school-based programmes to highly structured competitive leagues and, increasingly in some sports, early specialised development pathways aimed at identifying and nurturing future elite athletes from a young age.

Participation in youth sports is widely associated with a range of physical and social benefits for children, including improved fitness, motor skill development, teamwork and discipline, though researchers and coaches have raised growing concerns in recent decades about the risks of early sport specialisation, including burnout and higher rates of overuse injuries among young athletes who focus intensively on a single sport too early.

Many national sports federations and Olympic bodies now run dedicated youth development programmes, and events such as the Youth Olympic Games, first held in 2010, have been created specifically to give talented young athletes early experience of major international competition in a setting designed with their development in mind.

articles.title: Amateur Sport
articles.description: Sport for its own sake, outside professional competition.
articles.content:
Amateur sport refers to athletic competition undertaken primarily for enjoyment, personal fitness or love of the activity itself, rather than as a paid profession, though the boundary between amateur and professional sport has shifted considerably over the history of organised competition. The ancient Olympic Games were originally intended purely for amateur competitors, and this ideal strongly shaped the modern Olympic movement founded by Pierre de Coubertin in the late 19th century.

For much of the 20th century, many major sports, including Olympic competition itself, maintained strict rules barring professional athletes from taking part, though these restrictions were gradually relaxed from the 1970s and 1980s onward as the distinction became increasingly difficult to enforce and as sponsorship revenue transformed the finances of even nominally amateur competitors.

Today, amateur sport continues to thrive at community, school and recreational levels worldwide, providing the broad participatory base from which professional and Olympic-level athletes are often eventually drawn, even as elite competition itself has become almost entirely professionalised across most major sports.
